title: The Chess Champion
summary: A boy who just learned chess keeps losing to his older sister, but by studying his mistakes and practicing patiently, he plays a smart, hard-fought game at his school's chess tournament.
poll: Losing again and again at something new means you should probably give up and try something else instead.

versions.title: The Chess Champion
versions.text:
Khaled just learned to play chess. He has a king, a queen, and many other pieces. He plays on a board with small squares.

Khaled plays chess with his big sister, Sara. Sara is very good. Khaled loses every game. He feels sad.

Khaled wants to give up. But he does not quit. He looks at the board after each game. He thinks about his moves. What move was bad? He wants to learn.

Every day, Khaled practices. He moves his pieces slowly. He plans each move. He gets a little better each time.

The school has a chess club. The club plans a big match. Khaled signs up to play.

On the day of the match, Khaled sits at the board. His hands feel cold. He takes a deep breath. He thinks hard about each move.

The game is long and close. Khaled sees a smart move. He makes it. He wins the game!

Khaled smiles big. He worked hard, and it paid off.

versions.title: The Chess Champion
versions.text:
Khaled had just learned how to play chess. He loved the king, queen, and all the other pieces on the board. Still, he had a lot to learn. He often played against his big sister, Sara. Sara had played chess for years and understood far more strategy than he did. Every single time they played, Khaled lost. He began to feel pretty discouraged.

Part of Khaled wanted to give up on chess entirely. But instead of quitting, he decided to study each loss carefully. After every game against his opponent, he looked closely at the board. He asked himself exactly which move had been a mistake. Slowly, he started to understand why Sara always seemed to win.

Khaled practiced patiently every single day after school. He moved his pieces carefully and thought about his plans a few moves ahead. He tried not to repeat the same mistakes twice. Little by little, his games against Sara became closer, even though he still usually lost in the end.

That year, Khaled's school announced a chess tournament. Excitement spread quickly through the chess club. Khaled signed up right away, even though the thought of playing against other students made him nervous.

On the day of the tournament, Khaled sat down across from a tough, unfamiliar opponent. His hands felt cold, so he took a slow, deep breath before the game began. He thought carefully about every move, remembering everything he had learned from losing to Sara.

The match turned out to be long and incredibly close. Then Khaled suddenly noticed a clever move that his opponent had missed. He made the move carefully. After a tense, hard-fought struggle, he finally won the game.

Khaled grinned with pride. All those patient hours of studying his mistakes had truly paid off.

keyWords.definition: the flat object with squares that a game like chess is played on
keyWords.example: We set the checkers board on the kitchen table.

keyWords.example: In the story, the king piece stands in the middle of the back row.

keyWords.definition: one turn in which a player shifts a piece on the board

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A boy who buys a new chess set for his birthday and plays it with his friends
A boy who keeps losing at chess but learns to play better
A girl who teaches her whole class to play chess in a week
A family that goes on a trip together to the beach
questions.why: The story follows Khaled as he loses again and again, then learns from his mistakes and gets better at chess.

wrong.A: Khaled already has pieces; buying a set is not the story.
wrong.C: Sara does not teach the whole class in this story.
wrong.D: There is no family trip in this story.

questions.stem: Who does Khaled lose to every time at first?
options: A boy from the chess club
His teacher
His sister, Sara
His unfamiliar opponent at the tournament
questions.why: In the story, Khaled plays chess with his sister, Sara, and loses every game against her.

wrong.A: The club boy appears later, at the tournament, not at first.
wrong.B: No teacher plays chess with Khaled in the story.
wrong.D: The unfamiliar opponent is who Khaled faces at the tournament, not at first.

questions.stem: What does Khaled do after each loss to Sara?
options: He stops playing chess for good and goes home
He asks Sara to let him win the next game
He tells Sara the game was not fair and walks away
He looks at the board and thinks about his moves
questions.why: After each game, Khaled looks closely at the board and thinks about which move was bad.

wrong.A: Khaled keeps playing even after losing; he does not quit.
wrong.B: The story never says Khaled asks Sara to let him win.
wrong.C: Khaled never says the game was unfair.

questions.stem: In the story, a move is —
options: a type of chess piece that is shaped like a horse
one turn when a player moves a piece
the name of a chess club in a school
a square on the board where a king sits
questions.why: The story talks about Khaled thinking hard about each move, meaning each turn he takes in the game.

wrong.A: The king and queen are pieces, but a move is not a piece.
wrong.C: A move is not the name of a club.
wrong.D: A square is part of the board, not a move.

questions.stem: Why does Khaled keep practicing even though he loses to Sara every time?
options: He wants to make Sara feel bad about winning
His teacher makes him practice every single day
He wants to learn from his mistakes and get better
He has nothing else to do at home after school
questions.why: The story says Khaled wants to learn, so he looks at his moves and practices to slowly get better.

wrong.A: Khaled is not trying to upset Sara; he wants to improve.
wrong.B: No teacher is mentioned telling Khaled to practice.
wrong.D: The story does not say practicing is just something to fill time.

questions.stem: Why does the chess match on tournament day turn out to be close?
options: The other player does not know how to play
Khaled lets the other player win on purpose
The game only lasts for one minute
Khaled has practiced and gotten better at chess
questions.why: Because Khaled practiced and learned from his mistakes, he is skilled enough to make the match close and hard-fought.

wrong.A: The opponent is described as tough and skilled, not someone who cannot play.
wrong.B: Khaled plays his best to win, not to lose on purpose.
wrong.C: The story says the game is long, not short.

questions.stem: What happens right after Khaled sees the smart move at the tournament?
options: He makes the move and wins the game
He decides to stop playing
He asks for a new chess board
The other player quits the match
questions.why: After Khaled spots the smart move, he makes it carefully, and then he wins the game.

wrong.B: Khaled finishes the game instead of stopping.
wrong.C: No new board is mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: The opponent keeps playing until the match ends.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us that Khaled's hands feel cold before the tournament match?
options: To show that Khaled feels nervous before playing
To show that the room has no heating, so the hands are cold
To explain that Khaled is sick that day and cannot play
To show that Khaled does not want to play the match
questions.why: Cold, shaky hands show how nervous Khaled feels right before his important match.

wrong.B: The story never says anything about the room's heating.
wrong.C: The story does not say Khaled is sick.
wrong.D: Khaled signs up and plays his best; he does want to play.

keyWords.definition: a contest with several matches or games to find a winner
keyWords.example: Our school held a basketball tournament during spring break.

questions.stem: What is the best summary of this story?
options: A boy loses often at chess, studies his mistakes, and plays a smart match
A girl learns to swim after years of being afraid of water
A boy builds a new chessboard out of wood for his sister
A class takes a field trip to watch a professional chess tournament
questions.why: The story follows Khaled as he repeatedly loses, studies his mistakes, and finally plays a smart match at the tournament.

wrong.B: There is no swimming in this story.
wrong.C: Khaled never builds a chessboard in the story.
wrong.D: No field trip is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: What does Khaled do after every loss to his opponent, Sara?
options: He studies the board and looks for his mistake
He asks for a rematch right away without thinking
He throws the pieces off the board
He asks his teacher to explain the rules again
questions.why: After every loss, Khaled studies the board carefully and asks himself which move had been a mistake.

wrong.B: Khaled thinks carefully before playing again, instead of rushing.
wrong.C: The story never says Khaled throws the pieces.
wrong.D: No teacher is mentioned explaining rules in this story.

questions.stem: What does Khaled gradually begin to notice about Sara while he studies his losses?
options: That she always plays the same first move
That she gets nervous during every match
That she wins because of patterns in her strategy
That she secretly does not like playing chess
questions.why: The story says Khaled begins to notice patterns in Sara's strategy as he studies why she keeps winning.

wrong.A: The story never mentions Sara's first move.
wrong.B: The story does not describe Sara as nervous.
wrong.D: Nothing suggests Sara dislikes chess.

questions.stem: In the story, to be patient means to —
options: give up quickly when something feels hard
wait calmly and keep trying without giving up
play a game as fast as possible
get upset whenever you lose a match
questions.why: Khaled practices patiently every day, calmly trying again and again instead of giving up.

wrong.A: Khaled refuses to give up, which is the opposite of this.
wrong.C: Khaled thinks carefully, rather than rushing through moves.
wrong.D: Khaled stays calm and keeps trying instead of getting upset.

questions.stem: Why does Khaled's confidence likely grow in the weeks before the tournament?
options: His games against Sara keep becoming closer
Sara stops playing chess with him for weeks
His school cancels the chess club this year
He buys an expensive new chess set for the room
questions.why: As Khaled's games against Sara become noticeably closer, he can see that his careful practice is working.

wrong.B: Sara keeps playing chess with Khaled throughout the story.
wrong.C: The chess club is not canceled; it holds a tournament.
wrong.D: The story never mentions buying new equipment.

questions.stem: Why does Khaled feel nervous about competing in the tournament?
options: He will be playing against unfamiliar students he does not know
He has never seen a chessboard before and does not know the pieces
He is certain that he will win every match easily and feels proud
He does not understand how the pieces move on the board
questions.why: In the story, the thought of competing against unfamiliar students makes Khaled nervous about the outcome.

wrong.B: Khaled has played chess at home for a while already.
wrong.C: Khaled feels nervous, not overly confident.
wrong.D: Khaled clearly knows how the pieces move by this point.

questions.stem: What mainly causes Khaled to finally win his tournament match?
options: His opponent decides to quit early and goes home
He notices a clever move that his opponent missed
Sara secretly helps him from the sidelines with signs
The match is stopped before it finishes by the teacher
questions.why: Khaled wins because he notices a clever move that his opponent had completely missed and plays it carefully.

wrong.A: The opponent plays the whole match; the story does not say he quits.
wrong.C: Sara is not present helping Khaled during the tournament.
wrong.D: The match finishes after a tense, hard-fought struggle.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the events in this story?
options: By telling events in the order they happened, from Khaled's losses to his tournament win
By comparing chess rules in different countries around the world and over many years
By explaining, step by step, how to set up a chessboard for a new game
By listing reasons why chess is better than other games for children
questions.why: The story moves in time order: Khaled loses to Sara, studies his mistakes, practices, and then competes in the tournament.

wrong.B: The story never compares chess rules between countries.
wrong.C: The story does not explain how to set up a board.
wrong.D: The story never argues that chess is better than other games.

MID.prompt: Explain how studying his mistakes helps Khaled become a better chess player. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how studying his mistakes helped Khaled.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Studying his mistakes helps Khaled improve in a few important ways. After every loss to Sara, he looks closely at the board and asks himself which move was a costly mistake. Over time, he begins to notice patterns in Sara's strategy, which helps him understand why she keeps winning. Because he keeps learning from his mistakes instead of giving up, his games against Sara become closer, and he is finally ready to play a smart, hard-fought match at the tournament.

keyWords.definition: to examine something carefully in order to understand it fully
keyWords.example: Scientists analyze weather patterns to predict storms more accurately.

keyWords.definition: having made a firm decision to keep trying despite difficulty
keyWords.example: The determined climber kept going even after the trail grew steep.

keyWords.definition: relating to a careful plan aimed at achieving a long-term goal
keyWords.example: The coach made a strategic choice to rest her best player early in the game.

keyWords.definition: to think carefully and seriously about something that happened
keyWords.example: After the debate, the students were asked to reflect on their arguments.

keyWords.definition: able to recover quickly from difficulties and keep going
keyWords.example: Even after the storm destroyed their garden, the resilient family planted it again.

questions.stem: Which sentence best captures the central idea of this story?
options: A determined boy analyzes his losses and resiliently builds real strategic skill
A boy decides that chess is too difficult and switches to a different hobby
Two siblings argue constantly about which games are worth playing
A school eliminates its chess club because so few students join
questions.why: The story centers on Khaled analyzing his losses, practicing resiliently, and developing enough strategic skill to play a hard-fought match.

wrong.B: Khaled never gives up on chess for another hobby.
wrong.C: Khaled and Sara do not argue in this story.
wrong.D: The chess club thrives enough to hold a tournament.

questions.stem: What does Khaled specifically do after every disappointing loss to his opponent, Sara?
options: He reflects on the board to identify his costly mistake
He immediately challenges her to another match to win back
He asks their parents to intervene in the game next time
He decides the chess pieces are unfair and complains loudly
questions.why: After each loss, Khaled reflects thoughtfully on the board and identifies exactly which move had been a mistake.

wrong.B: Khaled studies first instead of rushing into another match.
wrong.C: No parents are mentioned getting involved in the story.
wrong.D: Khaled never blames the pieces themselves.

questions.stem: What specifically does Khaled gradually notice as he analyzes Sara's repeated victories?
options: Recurring patterns in her overall strategic approach
That Sara secretly practices with a different opponent
That the chessboard itself has a hidden flaw
That Sara always loses on purpose at first
questions.why: Through careful analysis, Khaled begins to notice recurring, predictable patterns in Sara's strategic approach to the game.

wrong.B: No other opponent for Sara is mentioned in the story.
wrong.C: Nothing in the story suggests a flawed board.
wrong.D: Sara wins consistently; she does not lose on purpose.

questions.stem: In the story, the word resilient most nearly means —
options: unable to continue after facing a setback or a mistake
quick to give up after a single failure in a game
able to recover and keep trying despite difficulty
uninterested in improving at all, even with a teacher
questions.why: Khaled practices resiliently, recovering from repeated losses and continuing to work toward improvement.

wrong.A: Khaled keeps going despite every setback.
wrong.B: Khaled does not give up after losing once.
wrong.D: Khaled clearly wants to improve, which this contradicts.

questions.stem: Why does competing against an unfamiliar opponent at the tournament provoke such nervousness in Khaled specifically?
options: Because he has never faced an opponent whose strategy he does not already know
Because he has forgotten the rules of chess entirely since last year
Because he dislikes everyone in the chess club and wants to leave
Because the tournament is held somewhere unfamiliar to him, far from his home town
questions.why: Having only studied Sara's strategy, Khaled naturally feels nervous facing an opponent whose patterns are unknown to him.

wrong.B: Khaled clearly remembers the rules and plays carefully.
wrong.C: Nothing suggests Khaled dislikes his fellow club members.
wrong.D: The story never mentions an unfamiliar location.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the role of Khaled's earlier losses to Sara in his eventual tournament win?
options: The losses taught him almost nothing useful for the tournament
The losses gave him the strategic experience he needed to win
The losses convinced him to quit chess before the tournament
The losses had no connection to the tournament at all
questions.why: By analyzing each loss to Sara, Khaled builds the exact strategic understanding he later uses to win his tournament match.

wrong.A: The losses teach him the patterns he later relies on.
wrong.C: Khaled remains determined and signs up for the tournament anyway.
wrong.D: The story directly connects his practice against Sara to his later success.

questions.stem: Which lists these events in the order they actually happened?
options: Khaled wins the tournament, he loses to Sara, he analyzes his mistakes
He analyzes his mistakes, he loses to Sara, the tournament is announced
The tournament is announced, he loses to Sara, he wins the tournament
He loses to Sara, he analyzes his mistakes, the tournament is announced, he wins
questions.why: Khaled first loses repeatedly to Sara, then analyzes his mistakes through practice, then the tournament is announced, and finally he wins his match.

wrong.A: Khaled cannot win the tournament before it is even announced.
wrong.B: Khaled loses to Sara before he can analyze those losses.
wrong.C: Khaled loses to Sara and analyzes his mistakes before the tournament is announced.

questions.stem: Why does the author emphasize how long and close the final tournament match becomes?
options: To suggest that Khaled's opponent was not trying very hard
To highlight how far Khaled's strategic skill had actually developed
To explain why the school decided to cancel future tournaments
To show that chess tournaments always last a long time
questions.why: A long, close match against a tough opponent shows just how much Khaled's patient analysis had improved his strategic play.

wrong.A: A tough, unfamiliar opponent suggests real effort, not a lack of it.
wrong.C: The story never mentions canceling future tournaments.
wrong.D: The story describes this one match, not every tournament ever held.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says losing again and again at something new means you should probably give up. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Khaled's losses, his analysis, and his tournament match.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that losing again and again means you should give up. Khaled lost to Sara every single time at first, yet he remained determined and analyzed each disappointing loss instead of quitting. Through patient, resilient practice, he began to notice recurring patterns in Sara's strategic approach, and that understanding carried directly into his tournament match. Someone might argue that repeated losing is simply discouraging and a sign to try something else, but Khaled's long, close, hard-fought victory shows that persistence and careful analysis can turn early failure into real improvement.

LOW.stem: What does the school chess club plan?
options: A trip to the sea
A big match
A new chess shop
A class party
LOW.why: In the story, the chess club is planning a big match.

wrong.A: A trip is not mentioned.
wrong.C: A shop is not mentioned.
wrong.D: A party is not mentioned.

LOW.stem: In the story, what does "quit" mean?
options: Play a game fast
Win a big prize
Ask for help
Stop doing something
LOW.why: Khaled wants to give up, but he does not quit, so he keeps trying.

wrong.A: Khaled plays slowly and plans, so fast play is not the meaning.
wrong.B: Winning a prize is not what quit means.
wrong.C: Asking for help is not what quit means.

LOW.stem: How does Khaled play when he practices?
options: He moves slowly and plans each move
He moves fast and does not plan
He plays only with his eyes closed
He plays without any pieces
LOW.why: The text says he moves his pieces slowly and plans each move.

wrong.B: He does the opposite: he plans and goes slowly.
wrong.C: The text says nothing about closing his eyes.
wrong.D: He uses the king, queen, and other pieces.

LOW.stem: What does Khaled do at the match that helps him win?
options: He plays very fast
He asks his sister what to do
He thinks hard about each move
He quits for a short time
LOW.why: He thinks hard about each move, and then he sees a smart move and wins.

wrong.A: He thinks hard, so he does not play fast.
wrong.B: His sister is not at the match in the story.
wrong.D: He does not quit; he stays and plays.

MID.stem: How long had Sara played chess?
options: Only for a day
For about a week
For a few months
For years
MID.why: The text says Sara had played chess for years.

wrong.A: A day is far too short; she knew far more strategy.
wrong.B: A week is far too short.
wrong.C: The text says years, not months.

MID.stem: In the story, the word "discouraged" means —
options: having less hope and confidence
feeling very proud and happy
being full of new ideas
wanting to play more games
MID.why: Khaled lost every game to Sara and felt discouraged, so he wanted to give up.

wrong.B: He was sad, not proud.
wrong.C: The sentence is about losing hope, not new ideas.
wrong.D: He wanted to give up chess, not play more.

MID.stem: Why did Khaled's games against Sara become closer?
options: Sara decided to stop playing her best chess
He played far fewer games with Sara each week
He practiced carefully and planned ahead every day
He moved to a much easier board
MID.why: He practiced every day, thought ahead, and tried not to repeat mistakes, so his games became closer.

wrong.A: Nothing says Sara played worse.
wrong.B: He practiced every day, not less.
wrong.D: The text never mentions a different board.

MID.stem: Why does the author say Khaled "still usually lost in the end"?
options: To show that Sara was a very cruel player
To show that he improved slowly, not all at once
To show that chess is far too hard to learn
To show that he should have quit chess
MID.why: His games were closer, but he still lost, which shows slow improvement over time.

wrong.A: The text does not call Sara cruel.
wrong.C: Khaled does learn chess by the end.
wrong.D: The story rewards him for not quitting.

HIGH.stem: How often did Khaled practice chess?
options: Only on weekends
Once a month
Every single day after school
Only before the tournament
HIGH.why: The text says he practiced every single day after school, refusing to skip even one session.

wrong.A: He practiced on school days, not only weekends.
wrong.B: Once a month is far too rarely for the text.
wrong.D: He practiced long before the tournament was announced.

HIGH.stem: In the story, the word "analyze" most nearly means —
options: to forget it quickly
to study closely to understand
to throw away
to play without much thinking
HIGH.why: Khaled looked at the board after each loss and asked which move was a mistake, so he examined it closely.

wrong.A: He remembered his losses to learn.
wrong.C: He kept his losses in mind, not threw them away.
wrong.D: He thought carefully about every move.

HIGH.stem: Why did Khaled sign up for the tournament even though he felt nervous?
options: He was determined to test his skills
His older sister made him join
He knew he would win very easily
The school gave him a prize for joining
HIGH.why: In the text, he signed up right away, determined to test his improving skills.

wrong.B: The text does not say Sara made him.
wrong.C: He felt nervous, so he did not expect an easy win.
wrong.D: No prize for joining is mentioned.

HIGH.stem: What does the sentence about Khaled waiting, "determined not to let the opportunity slip away," show?
options: He was too scared to move any piece at all
He forgot what to do next in the long game
He wanted the long game to end soon
He stayed patient and focused at a key moment
HIGH.why: He noticed a clever move and waited carefully, which shows patience and focus.

wrong.A: He made the move carefully, so he was not frozen.
wrong.B: He knew the clever move, so he did not forget.
wrong.C: He kept playing through a long, close match.
